newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asian Grain- S.Korean interest in wheat perks up.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain- S.Korean interest in wheat perks up.

text.p: South Korean interest in wheat purchases is increasing on a a bearish outlook for international prices due to the approach of the U.S. winter wheat harvest and recent improvements in crop condition ratings, local traders said on Monday.
"Some of our clients said they are considering inviting tenders to buy U.S. wheat for August shipment during this week," a trader with a major wheat supplier in Seoul said.

The wheat trader said Cheiljedang and Dongah Flour Mills Co Ltd are expected to jointly seek about 20,000 tonnes and Daehan Flour Mills Co Ltd is also likely to buy 20,000 tonnes, both for August shipments to the western port of Inchon.
Other traders said the bearish outlook for the wheat market was supported by recent favourable crop weather in Europe and Australia, as well as the U.S.

Meanwhile, several South Korean corn buyer groups were seen seeking one or two 50,000-tonne cargoes for arrival in September, but they were in no hurry to cover their requirements as they expct Chicago prices to fall further, traders said.
They added buyers, who had been looking for October arrival onward, were also seen out of the market as corn crop prospects improve with favourable conditions in the U.S. Midwest.
In Japan, grain importers said they have covered up to 80 percent of their U.S. corn requirements for the July-September shipment, and are waiting for the right timing to buy the rest.
Japan's corn premiums were seen at 92 to 93 U.S. cents a bushel over CBOT July futures, against 93 U.S. cents last week.

"We've bought up to 80 percent (of U.S. corn requirement). The point now is when we should buy the rest," one corn trader said. "Some trade houses will launch buying this week, partly due to the firmer tone in freight rates."
Nearby freight rates on the U.S. Gulf/Japan route were quoted at slightly above US$21 a tonne, traders said.
"The freight rate is firming gradually, and will encourage importers to cover U.S. grain this week," a corn trader said.

An official with South Korea's Pan Ocean Shipping Co Ltd said freight rates from the Pacific Northwest to the country were flat at $12 a tonne over the past week for Panamax-sized cargoes for nearby shipment.

But rates from the U.S. Gulf for further forward for mid-June to July, on the same basis, fell to $20.50 a tonne from $22 a week ago due to slightly reduced demand for grain vessels out of the Gulf region.

Traders said this was due to an increase in corn shipments from China and South America to South Korea in mid-year which had reduced offtake from the U.S. and consequent demand for vessels from this origin.
